text:
## Abstract  
We quantified the volume and major data types available for the human pathogen Staphylococcus aureus in two widely-used public repositories: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) for processed functional genomic data and the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) for raw sequencing reads. Using the geo_search tool we retrieved the total number of GEO Series (GSE) and Sample (GSM) records annotated with the organism tag “Staphylococcus aureus”. For ENA, the brc_ena_runs and brc_ena_search tools provided the overall run count for taxon 1280 as well as counts for four common library strategies (WGS, RNA-Seq, AMPLICON, ChIP-Seq). GEO contains 500 Series and 5 464 Samples, whereas ENA stores 181 408 sequencing runs. Within ENA, whole-genome sequencing (WGS) dominates (171 172 runs, 94.4 %), followed by RNA-Seq (6 465; 3.6 %), amplicon (1 219; 0.7 %) and ChIP-Seq (28; 0.02 %). These figures illustrate complementary but very different scopes: GEO emphasises curated, processed expression and functional studies, while ENA concentrates on primary sequence data, predominantly WGS. Understanding this distinction helps researchers choose the most appropriate repository for data mining or submission.

## I. Introduction  
Background. Staphylococcus aureus is a major human pathogen responsible for a spectrum of diseases ranging from minor skin infections to life-threatening sepsis. Public archives such as GEO and ENA underpin genomic and functional studies by providing access to processed and raw data, respectively.  
Literature Review. No literature was retrieved for this query.  
Knowledge Gap. The relative scale and composition of S. aureus datasets across GEO and ENA have not been directly compared in a quantitative manner.  
Objective & Hypothesis. We aimed to compare the quantity and primary data-type composition of S. aureus records in GEO versus ENA, expecting ENA to house a larger volume of raw sequencing runs, while GEO would hold fewer but more processed expression studies.

## II. Materials and Methods  
Study Design. Counts were obtained independently from GEO (processed expression archives) and ENA (raw read archive) using repository-specific APIs exposed through the MCP tools.  
Materials.  
• GEO via geo_search (NCBI E-utilities)  
• ENA via brc_ena_runs and brc_ena_search (BRC Analytics proxy to ENA)  
Procedures.  
1. GEO Series (GSE) count  
   – geo_search(organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gse", max_results=1)  
   – URL: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gse%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
2. GEO Sample (GSM) count  
   – geo_search(organism="Staphylococcus aureus", entry_type="gsm", max_results=1)  
   – URL: https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gsm%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
3. ENA total runs  
   – brc_ena_runs(taxonomy_id="1280", limit=1)  
   – URL: https://brc-analytics.org/api/v1/ena/taxonomy/1280?limit=1  
4. ENA runs by library strategy  
   – brc_ena_search(taxonomy_id="1280", library_strategy="WGS", limit=1)  
   – brc_ena_search(taxonomy_id="1280", library_strategy="RNA-Seq", limit=1)  
   – brc_ena_search(taxonomy_id="1280", library_strategy="AMPLICON", limit=1)  
   – brc_ena_search(taxonomy_id="1280", library_strategy="ChIP-Seq", limit=1)  
   – Corresponding URLs are listed in References.  
Statistical Analysis. The “total_count” field from GEO responses and “total_in_ena” or “total_matching” fields from ENA responses were extracted. Percentages were calculated as (strategy-specific runs ÷ total ENA runs) × 100, rounded to one decimal place.

## III. Results  
Data Presentation.  

Table 1. GEO records for Staphylococcus aureus  
| GEO entry type | Total records |
|---|---|
| Series (GSE) | 500 |
| Samples (GSM) | 5 464 |

Table 2. ENA sequencing runs for Staphylococcus aureus (taxid 1280)  
| Library strategy | Runs | Proportion of ENA total (%) |
|---|---|---|
| All strategies (total) | 181 408 | 100.0 |
| WGS | 171 172 | 94.4 |
| RNA-Seq | 6 465 | 3.6 |
| AMPLICON | 1 219 | 0.7 |
| ChIP-Seq | 28 | 0.02 |

Findings. GEO stores 500 curated Series encompassing 5 464 Samples for S. aureus. ENA contains 181 408 raw sequencing runs; the majority (94.4 %) are whole-genome sequencing, with smaller fractions for RNA-Seq (3.6 %), amplicon (0.7 %) and ChIP-Seq (0.02 %).

## IV. Discussion  
Interpretation. The data confirm that ENA is the principal repository for raw S. aureus sequencing, dominated by WGS datasets, whereas GEO offers a comparatively modest collection focused on processed functional studies.  
Context. The disparity reflects each repository’s remit: ENA archives primary sequence reads, while GEO curates experiment-level expression and functional genomics outputs.  
Limitations. Counts rely on organism annotations that may omit mis-annotated records. GEO experiment-type filters were not fully enumerated; additional profiling categories could raise the GEO counts. ENA strategy counts were limited to four common categories; other strategies (e.g., Hi-C, ATAC-Seq) were not queried.  
Conclusion & Future Directions. Researchers seeking large-scale genomic diversity or raw data should consult ENA, whereas GEO remains useful for curated expression and binding studies. Further work could profile additional ENA library strategies and classify GEO Series by assay type to refine cross-repository comparisons.

## References  
[1] NCBI GEO Series count for Staphylococcus aureus. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gse%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[2] NCBI GEO Sample count for Staphylococcus aureus. https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=gds&term=%22Staphylococcus%20aureus%22%5BOrganism%5D%20AND%20%22gsm%22%5BFilter%5D&retmax=1  
[3] ENA total runs for taxid 1280. https://brc-analytics.org/api/v1/ena/taxonomy/1280?limit=1  
[4] ENA WGS runs for taxid 1280. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?query=tax_eq(1280)%20AND%20library_strategy=%22WGS%22&limit=1  
[5] ENA RNA-Seq runs for taxid 1280. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?query=tax_eq(1280)%20AND%20library_strategy=%22RNA-Seq%22&limit=1  
[6] ENA AMPLICON runs for taxid 1280. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?query=tax_eq(1280)%20AND%20library_strategy=%22AMPLICON%22&limit=1  
[7] ENA ChIP-Seq runs for taxid 1280. https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/portal/api/search?query=tax_eq(1280)%20AND%20library_strategy=%22ChIP-Seq%22&limit=1  

## Acknowledgments  
We thank NCBI GEO and the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) via BRC Analytics for open access to their records.

Statistical Analysis. The “total_count” field from GEO responses and “total_in_ena” or “total_matching” fields from ENA responses were extracted. Percentages were calculated as (strategy-specific runs ÷ total ENA runs) × 100, rounded to one decimal place.

## III. Results  
Data Presentation.  

Table 1. GEO records for Staphylococcus aureus  
| GEO entry type | Total records |
|---|---|
| Series (GSE) | 500 |
| Samples (GSM) | 5 464 |

Table 2. ENA sequencing runs for Staphylococcus aureus (taxid 1280)  
| Library strategy | Runs | Proportion of ENA total (%) |
|---|---|---|
| All strategies (total) | 181 408 | 100.0 |
| WGS | 171 172 | 94.4 |
| RNA-Seq | 6 465 | 3.6 |
| AMPLICON | 1 219 | 0.7 |
| ChIP-Seq | 28 | 0.02 |

Findings. GEO stores 500 curated Series encompassing 5 464 Samples for S. aureus. ENA contains 181 408 raw sequencing runs; the majority (94.4 %) are whole-genome sequencing, with smaller fractions for RNA-Seq (3.6 %), amplicon (0.7 %) and ChIP-Seq (0.02 %).

## IV. Discussion  
Interpretation. The data confirm that ENA is the principal repository for raw S. aureus sequencing, dominated by WGS datasets, whereas GEO offers a comparatively modest collection focused on processed functional studies.  
Context. The disparity reflects each repository’s remit: ENA archives primary sequence reads, while GEO curates experiment-level expression and functional genomics outputs.  
Limitations. Counts rely on organism annotations that may omit mis-annotated records. GEO experiment-type filters were not fully enumerated; additional profiling categories could raise the GEO counts. ENA strategy counts were limited to four common categories; other strategies (e.g., Hi-C, ATAC-Seq) were not queried.  
Conclusion & Future Directions. Researchers seeking large-scale genomic diversity or raw data should consult ENA, whereas GEO remains useful for curated expression and binding studies. Further work could profile additional ENA library strategies and classify GEO Series by assay type to refine cross-repository comparisons.
